notes:
Task and constraints: Apply find-and-replace operations to a string when each source matches at its original index.
Idea: Precompute valid replacements at source indices, then scan the original string and emit replacement text or the original character.
Technique and why it applies: A bucket stores replacement length and target characters, letting the output scan skip matched source spans without shifting future indices.
Invariant: bucket[i] describes a valid replacement beginning at original position i.
Edge cases: The source check bounds each character index, but assumes operations do not conflict at the same index; later assignments overwrite earlier bucket entries.
Complexity: Validation and output construction take O(n+total source lengths+output length) time and O(n+output) space.

Task and constraints: For each tree node, return the sum of its distances to all other nodes.
Idea: Build an undirected tree, run postorder to compute subtree sizes and root distances, then preorder to reroot distance sums.
Technique and why it applies: Moving the root across an edge decreases distances to the child's subtree by its size and increases distances to all other nodes by their count.
Invariant: tree_nodes stores subtree sizes and distances stores the distance sum for the current root.
Edge cases: The tree is assumed connected and acyclic; recursive DFS may hit Python's recursion limit for a long chain.
Complexity: Two traversals take O(n) time and O(n) adjacency plus recursion space.

Task and constraints: Compute the sum of distances from every node to all other nodes in a tree.
Idea: Use one DFS to calculate subtree sizes and root-distance sums, then reroot those sums through a second DFS.
Technique and why it applies: For child v of u, result[v] equals result[u] minus count[v] plus the number of nodes outside v's subtree.
Invariant: count stores subtree sizes and result stores distance totals for each root.
Edge cases: The code assumes a valid tree and uses recursive traversal, which can exceed recursion limits on deep trees.
Complexity: The adjacency construction and two traversals take O(N) time and O(N) space.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum overlap between two binary images under translation.
Idea: Collect coordinates of ones in both images and count every relative displacement between a pair of ones.
Technique and why it applies: Each pair contributes to the translation that aligns those two cells; the most frequent displacement gives the largest overlap.
Invariant: shiftDict maps row-column offsets to the number of aligned one-pairs.
Edge cases: defaultdict is referenced without an import in the snippet, so it needs external definition. If either image has no ones, the method returns zero.
Complexity: With a ones in the first image and b in the second, time is O(ab+N²), and space is O(ab) possible shifts.

Task and constraints: Find the largest overlap between two binary images by trying all one-cell pairs.
Idea: For every one in A and every one in B, increment a bucket for their relative translation.
Technique and why it applies: The offset maps one coordinate pair onto the other; its count equals the overlap produced by that translation.
Invariant: count stores pair counts for each possible row-column displacement.
Edge cases: The grid is assumed square and both images have matching dimensions. If no pair of ones exists, all buckets remain zero.
Complexity: The nested scans take O(N⁴) time and O(N²) space for displacement buckets.

Task and constraints: Determine whether two axis-aligned rectangles overlap with positive area.
Idea: Check whether one rectangle lies entirely to the left, right, above, or below the other.
Technique and why it applies: If any separating condition holds, overlap is false; touching edges count as non-overlap.
Invariant: The conditional tests whether projections are separated on either axis.
Edge cases: Coordinates are assumed to be valid rectangle bounds; equality at an edge is treated as no overlap.
Complexity: Only four comparisons are needed, so time and auxiliary space are O(1).

Task and constraints: Check whether two rectangles have positive-area intersection.
Idea: Use a helper to test interval overlap on the horizontal and vertical projections.
Technique and why it applies: The intervals intersect only when max(left endpoints) is strictly less than min(right endpoints); both axes must overlap.
Invariant: intersect evaluates one-dimensional overlap, and the final conjunction requires both dimensions.
Edge cases: Rectangles that merely touch at an edge or corner return false because the comparison is strict.
Complexity: The method uses O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the probability of finishing the New 21 Game with a score no greater than n.
Idea: Use a sliding-window DP over terminal probabilities for scores from k through k+maxPts-1.
Technique and why it applies: The probability for a score is the average of the next maxPts outcomes; the running sum updates the window as scores move downward.
Invariant: dp stores probabilities for a consecutive range of future scores, and s is their sum.
Edge cases: collections.deque is used without an import in the snippet. The deque size remains maxPts during the recurrence.
Complexity: The loop takes O(k+maxPts) time and O(maxPts) space.

Task and constraints: Simulate domino falls spreading left or right until forces settle.
Idea: Process falling dominoes in BFS layers, accumulating signed pushes from left and right.
Technique and why it applies: A location reached by opposing directions receives both signs; zero remains upright, while the sign determines the final direction.
Invariant: arr stores net directional force and d tracks locations already assigned to a wave.
Edge cases: The code uses sets to merge positions reached within a layer; correctness depends on each layer representing equal-time arrivals.
Complexity: Each position is processed a bounded number of times, giving O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Determine the final orientation of each domino after all pushes settle.
Idea: Scan left-to-right to accumulate rightward force and right-to-left to accumulate leftward force.
Technique and why it applies: Rightward force decreases with distance and resets at R or L; the reverse scan applies the symmetric rule, and the net sign determines the result.
Invariant: force stores the signed difference between left and right influence at each position.
Edge cases: Existing L and R dominoes reset the sweep, and positions with equal forces remain upright.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Count groups of strings connected by pairwise similarity, where similar strings differ at no more than two positions.
Idea: Run DFS over string indices, connecting each unvisited string similar to the current one.
Technique and why it applies: Each DFS discovers one connected component in the implicit similarity graph.
Invariant: visited records explored indices, and count increments once for each new component.
Edge cases: The implementation's isSimilar accepts any pair differing in at most two positions; for anagrams, the problem's exactly-two swap relation also requires equal character multisets, assumed by the input.
Complexity: Pairwise comparisons make time O(n²L), where L is string length, and space O(n).

Task and constraints: Count 3-by-3 magic squares inside a grid.
Idea: For each candidate window, check row sums, column sums, both diagonal sums, distinct entries, and minimum value one.
Technique and why it applies: Every row and column and both diagonals must equal the expected sum; nine distinct values starting at one then force the values 1 through 9.
Invariant: magic validates a candidate square and the outer loops count valid windows.
Edge cases: The code sets k=3 as required. The sum checks and uniqueness/minimum conditions establish the normal 1-to-9 constraints.
Complexity: Each window takes O(1) work for fixed size, so overall time is O(RC) and extra space O(1).

Task and constraints: Determine whether all rooms can be visited starting from room zero using keys.
Idea: Run breadth-first search, enqueueing every key found in a newly visited room.
Technique and why it applies: A key reveals an edge to another room; visited tracking prevents repeatedly processing rooms and cycles.
Invariant: visited_rooms records discovered rooms, and queue holds rooms awaiting processing.
Edge cases: collections is referenced without an import in the snippet. The method assumes at least one room because room zero is queued initially.
Complexity: Each room and key is processed at most once, giving O(V+E) time and O(V) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether every room is reachable from room zero.
Idea: Use a stack-based graph traversal and mark each newly discovered room before pushing it.
Technique and why it applies: Keys act as directed edges from a room to rooms it opens; the visited set prevents duplicate work.
Invariant: lookup contains discovered rooms, and stack contains rooms still to explore.
Edge cases: For a single room, the loop is skipped and the final equality returns true. The early success return occurs when all rooms are discovered.
Complexity: Traversal takes O(V+E) time and O(V) space.

Task and constraints: Split a digit string into a Fibonacci-like integer sequence within the 32-bit bound.
Idea: Try possible first and second numbers, then recursively consume the remaining string using the sum of the previous two values.
Technique and why it applies: The next expected integer must match the start of the remaining suffix; leading-zero checks prevent invalid multi-digit terms.
Invariant: current holds the sequence so far and consume_tail advances through matching decimal prefixes.
Edge cases: The constant MAX is 2**31, but the usual bound is 2**31-1, so the code allows one value beyond the strict limit. Recursion can be deep.
Complexity: The candidate-prefix search is exponential in the worst case, with recursion proportional to sequence length.

Task and constraints: Find a Fibonacci-like sequence that consumes the entire digit string.
Idea: Try first and second numbers, then repeatedly parse the exact sum of the last two terms from the remaining digits.
Technique and why it applies: startswith builds the next decimal number and stops once it exceeds the expected sum; success requires consuming all digits.
Invariant: fib stores the current sequence and k marks the next unconsumed character.
Edge cases: Leading zero handling is enforced by breaking when a first or second term starts with zero and grows beyond one digit.
Complexity: The search has exponential worst-case branching, while each successful sequence uses O(n) storage.

Task and constraints: Compare two strings after applying backspaces represented by #.
Idea: Generate each final string backward while counting pending deletions, then compare the resulting character streams.
Technique and why it applies: A # increases deletion debt; ordinary characters consume debt before being yielded, avoiding construction of edited strings.
Invariant: backwardResult yields surviving characters in reverse order.
Edge cases: zip_longest is referenced without an import, so the snippet needs external definition. Unequal lengths of final streams compare false via fill values.
Complexity: The two strings are scanned O(|s|+|t|) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond generators.

Task and constraints: Check whether two strings are equal after backspace processing.
Idea: Scan both strings from right to left, skipping characters erased by pending # symbols.
Technique and why it applies: findNextChar yields only characters that survive backspaces; zip_longest compares all yielded positions, including unequal lengths.
Invariant: skip counts pending backspaces while each generator moves backward through its input.
Edge cases: The code imports itertools and handles strings that reduce to empty; differing final lengths fail comparison.
Complexity: Time is O(|S|+|T|) and auxiliary space is O(1) beyond generator state.

Task and constraints: Find the longest contiguous mountain: strictly increasing then strictly decreasing with both sides nonempty.
Idea: Build increasing-run and decreasing-run lengths for each index, then combine them at candidate peaks.
Technique and why it applies: A valid peak needs an increasing length and decreasing length both greater than one; subtract one because the peak is counted twice.
Invariant: max_up and max_down store run lengths ending and starting at each position.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return zero; equal adjacent values break both mountain sides.
Complexity: Two scans and a final maximum take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the longest mountain in an array using rolling ascent and descent lengths.
Idea: Scan adjacent pairs, resetting after a flat step or an ascent following a descent.
Technique and why it applies: A mountain is complete when both an ascent and descent have positive lengths; their sum plus one gives its length.
Invariant: up_len and down_len track the current ascending and descending edges.
Edge cases: Equal adjacent values reset the candidate; an ascent after a descent starts a new mountain rather than extending the old one.
Complexity: The single pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
